questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between extractables and leachables?

options.A: Leachables are substances extracted by solvents under accelerated laboratory conditions; extractables are foreign substances actually detected in the drug product
options.B: Leachables are generally a subset of, or derived from, extractables and migrate into the drug product during normal storage and use or accelerated stability testing
options.C: The two are non-overlapping groups; leachables come only from secondary and tertiary packaging, and extractables only from primary packaging
options.D: Extractables are limited to organic compounds released from packaging materials; leachables include both organic and inorganic chemical entities

questions.explanation: Extractables are organic and inorganic substances released into an extraction solvent under laboratory conditions; they or their derivatives may migrate into the drug product and become leachables, so leachables are generally a subset of, or derived from, extractables. The option that swaps the two definitions is wrong; substances from secondary and tertiary packaging are migrants, which is not the definition of leachables.

questions.question: According to the USP ⟨1663⟩ definition, what is the source of migrants?

options.A: Additives naturally released over the shelf life from primary packaging components in direct contact with the drug product, such as IV bags and rubber stoppers
options.B: Substances remaining on contact surfaces of pharmaceutical equipment, such as filters, tubing and tanks, that are carried into the finished product during processing
options.C: Foreign chemical substances produced by degradation of the active ingredient and excipients in the formulation during storage
options.D: Substances from secondary and tertiary packaging and ancillary components that cross a physical barrier and enter the drug product

questions.explanation: Migrants are foreign substances present in the drug product after crossing a physical barrier; they originate from secondary and tertiary packaging and ancillary components (such as pallets and shrink wrap). Substances released from primary packaging in direct contact with the drug product fall within the scope of leachables.

questions.question: A team wants to use an extraction study to simulate the worst-case leachables profile. According to USP ⟨1663⟩, what is the most reasonable choice of extracting medium?

options.A: Use the drug product formulation itself first; if not feasible, use the drug product vehicle (placebo); only then a justified simulating solvent
options.B: Always use unbuffered purified water, because its simple composition makes results from different batches easiest to compare and reproduce and to exchange between laboratories
options.C: Always use an organic solvent such as hexane, because it has the strongest extracting power, covers everything the formulation itself could extract, and is independent of formulation composition
options.D: Replace the formulation with a pH 6.5 buffer, because this pH is closest to most injectable products and the extracting power of the formulation itself no longer needs to be considered

questions.explanation: Of all extraction parameters, the extracting medium is the most critical. To simulate the worst-case leachables profile, the most reasonable choice is to use the formulation directly, followed by the placebo. When a simulating solvent is needed, its composition must be established and justified according to all the physicochemical properties of the formulation that affect "extracting power", rather than always using water or an organic solvent.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1663⟩ Extractables Assessment › GENERATING THE EXTRACT › Chemical Nature of the Extracting Medium

questions.question: What is the main purpose of raising the temperature in a simulating extraction study?

options.A: To break extractables down into smaller molecules at high temperature, simplifying later identification and lowering the sensitivity and sample amount the analytical method requires
options.B: To ensure that extraction always reaches equilibrium in a short time, so there is no need to monitor during the study whether each extractable has reached an asymptotic or stable concentration
options.C: To increase the extraction rate so that a shorter study time can simulate a longer leaching time; the relationship between rate and temperature can be expressed by the Arrhenius equation
options.D: To reduce the extracting power of the extraction medium so that results are closer to normal storage conditions, while also reducing the total amount and number of extractables obtained

questions.explanation: Raising the temperature accelerates the extraction (diffusion) rate so that a short study can simulate long-term leaching, and the relationship between rate and temperature can be expressed by the Arrhenius equation. Even at elevated temperature, the extraction profile should still be monitored to see whether equilibrium or an asymptotic value has been reached, so the statement that equilibrium is always reached and monitoring is unnecessary is wrong.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1663⟩ Extractables Assessment › GENERATING THE EXTRACT › Extraction Time and Temperature

questions.question: In the USP ⟨1663⟩ example for a vial containing 5 mL of drug product, how should the study be designed to use stoichiometry to obtain a more concentrated extract?

options.A: Place 1 rubber stopper in 5 mL of extraction solvent, so that the solvent volume is exactly the same as the actual drug product volume, with no scaling up
options.B: Place 20 rubber stoppers in 2000 mL of extraction solvent, using a large solvent volume to ensure complete extraction and avoid saturation of the extract
options.C: Place 5 rubber stoppers in 200 mL of extraction solvent, keeping a simple fixed ratio between the number of stoppers and the drug product volume
options.D: Place 20 rubber stoppers in 200 mL of extraction solvent, increasing the ratio of sample to solvent volume

questions.explanation: Stoichiometry refers to the ratio of sample mass or surface area to extraction medium volume, which can be deliberately increased to obtain a more concentrated extract; the example is 20 stoppers in 200 mL of solvent (corresponding to a vial containing 5 mL of drug product). The other options are not the design described in the example, and a ratio of 1 stopper to 5 mL of solvent gives no concentrating effect.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1663⟩ Extractables Assessment › GENERATING THE EXTRACT › Extraction Stoichiometry

questions.question: Which statement about the Safety Concern Threshold (SCT) and the Analytical Evaluation Threshold (AET) is correct?

options.A: The SCT is the dose threshold below which safety concern is negligible; the AET is the analytical threshold above which substances should be identified and reported for toxicological assessment, and can be derived from the SCT
options.B: The AET is the dose threshold below which safety concern is negligible; the SCT is the lowest concentration an instrument can detect, determined by the sensitivity of the analytical method
options.C: The SCT and AET are the same fixed value, independent of the product's dosing parameters, and the same µg/day value is applied to all drug products and dosage forms
options.D: The AET is the maximum acceptable limit for each leachable at drug product release; the SCT is the lower limit at which analysts decide whether to continue scanning the extract

questions.explanation: The SCT is the safety-based threshold: a leachable below it is at such a low dose that carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic toxicity concerns are negligible. The AET is the analytical threshold: leachables at or above it should be identified and reported for toxicological assessment, and it can be derived mathematically from the SCT using factors such as dose, so the two are not the same value.

questions.question: Which of the following analyses is scouting, used to obtain information on the bulk properties of the extract?

options.A: Comparing the GC/MS mass spectrum and retention time with an authentic reference compound to confirm the structure of an individual extractable
options.B: Measuring TOC in an aqueous extract to gauge the total amount of organic extractables, optionally together with NVR and UV to interpret overall characteristics
options.C: Calibrating with an authentic reference compound as an external standard to convert to the concentration of each individual extractable in the extract
options.D: Using HPLC with MS detection to separate and locate the peaks and signals corresponding to individual organic compounds in the extract

questions.explanation: Scouting uses techniques such as UV, FTIR, NVR, ROI, pH and TOC to understand the overall nature and magnitude of the extractables; scouting alone cannot meet the practical goals of extract characterization. Confirming structure by GC/MS comparison is identification, converting to concentration with an external standard is quantitation, and separating and locating individual peaks by HPLC/MS is discovery; all three target individual extractables.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1663⟩ Extractables Assessment › CHARACTERIZING THE EXTRACT › Processes Involved in Extract Characterization

questions.question: According to USP ⟨1663⟩, what evidence is needed for the identification of an extractable to reach the "Confirmed" level?

options.A: Analytical data are consistent only with a class of molecules, and other clearly different classes of compounds have been excluded, but no additional evidence has been obtained
options.B: Additional and sufficient corroborating information on top of the tentative identification, giving the structural inference considerable confidence and support
options.C: The overall weight of evidence is sufficient for confirmation, and both the mass spectrum and the retention time match an authentic reference compound
options.D: Assignment of the chemical class from UV absorption and FTIR features, cross-checked against extraction profiles recorded for previous batches

questions.explanation: Identification confidence has three levels: Tentative is consistent only with a class of molecules; Confident is tentative plus sufficient corroborating information; Confirmed requires that the overall weight of evidence confirms the identity, with the mass spectrum and retention time matching an authentic reference compound. "Consistent only with a class of molecules" is Tentative, and "additional corroborating information" is Confident.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1663⟩ Extractables Assessment › CHARACTERIZING THE EXTRACT › Processes Involved in Extract Characterization

questions.question: For a high-risk drug product with a very stringent safety threshold (such as 0.15 µg/day), what does USP ⟨1663⟩ say an extractables assessment should include to be considered complete?

options.A: Multiple media of differing extracting power, multiple complementary extraction techniques including the ability to capture volatiles, and conditions that allow extraction to reach equilibrium
options.B: Soxhlet extraction with a single solvent, with extended reflux time until the concentration of extractables in the solvent no longer increases
options.C: Scouting only with NVR and pH, and considering the work complete once all results are confirmed to be below the material-based threshold values
options.D: Only one analytical technique, GC/MS, with a larger injection volume to improve sensitivity so that low-concentration extractables can also be detected

questions.explanation: Completeness can only be judged against the overall objective. A high-risk product requires multiple media of different extracting power, multiple complementary extraction techniques (including for volatiles) and conditions that reach equilibrium, together with multiple complementary analytical techniques and a systematic identification and quantitation process. A single solvent, a single technique or scouting alone is not sufficient.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1663⟩ Extractables Assessment › SUMMARY › Assessing the Completeness of an Extractables Assessment

questions.question: To evaluate volatile organic compounds released from cartons or rubber components when the contact scenario is not mediated by a solution, which class of technique is most suitable?

options.A: Maceration (solvent soaking), soaking the sample in an organic or aqueous solvent below its boiling point and then analyzing the solution
options.B: Soxhlet extraction, placing the sample in a Soxhlet apparatus where the solvent is repeatedly redistilled and refluxed, then analyzing the solution
options.C: Sealed vessel extraction, sealing the sample and solvent in a container and heating with steam in a laboratory autoclave
options.D: Volatiles-specific methods such as headspace GC, direct thermal desorption (TD/GC) or TGA/GC

questions.explanation: Not every contact scenario is solution-mediated; for volatile organic compounds, dedicated techniques include headspace (HD/GC), direct thermal desorption (TD/GC) and TGA/GC. Maceration, Soxhlet and sealed vessel extraction are all common solvent-mediated extraction techniques.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1663⟩ Extractables Assessment › GENERATING THE EXTRACT › Extractions That are Not Solvent Mediated
